title: How would you define an "AI-native" game?
author: MakeEmMayhem
selftext:
Hey everyone! A long-time quiet lurker here haha. Recently I’ve been thinking about the phrase “AI-native game.”



A lot of games now use AI somewhere in the pipeline: concept art, writing help, prototyping, NPC dialogue, asset generation, etc. But I’m not sure that automatically makes the game “AI-native.”



To me, an AI-native game would mean AI changes the actual player experience or core loop, not just how the game was made.



For example:

\- The player can create something the system actually understands

\- Characters or mechanics can adapt in meaningful ways

\- The strategy space changes because generated content affects decisions

\- The game would feel fundamentally different without AI



Do you guys think “AI-native game” is a real category yet? If yes, what games come closest?

comments.author: Apalala__
comments.body:
i guess it means,   
the game is design with AI in mind

comments.author: count023
comments.body:
AI native to me means it needs an LLM somewhre int eh actual execution of the game, be it a dialogue generator or some sort of graphics overlay (the new AI DLSS stuff is ai native to me because it requires that ai integration to look "optimal"), stuff like that. 

If it uses AI to function in the final product state, it's AI native. If you just use AI to help produce the content bu there's no AI in the game engine, then it's just ai developed/ai assisted.

replies.author: MakeEmMayhem
replies.body:
This is similar to the conclusion I’ve been coming to too.

If AI only helped make assets before launch, I’d call that AI-assisted. Useful, but not AI-native.

AI-native (to me) means the final player experience depends on AI being part of the system.

Small disclosure: I’m working on Make’Em Mayhem, an AI-native autobattler where players generate playable characters and the game turns them into units with personalities, abilities, strengths, weaknesses, and builds. So this definition is very close to how we think about it.

The interesting part is that AI changes the player’s role: you’re not just picking from a fixed roster, you’re helping create part of the roster.

replies.author: fungnoth
replies.body:
I would think of games that dynamically creates new content with ai. The easiest one would be npc dialog, the story / events can still be steered programmatically, but i would imagine the LLM would express the same thing differently.

And then it must be possible to have actual dynamic story, but I can't imagine it to be reliably interesting. That's the next level.

And then maybe gameplay elements that's other than text, like maps? props?

replies.author: MakeEmMayhem
replies.body:
Yeah! In Make'Em Mayhem, we want to take things to the next level. The idea is that players generate characters from their own prompts, and those characters come with personalities, weapons, abilities, strengths, and weaknesses that match the concept.  
  
So the AI is not just generating flavor text or visuals. It changes what you can actually build around. If your idea becomes a playable unit, then your creativity affects the strategy space directly. That’s the part my team finds exciting about AI-native games!

  
You can check out our gameplay trailer here!: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4424310/MakeEm\_Mayhem](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4424310/MakeEm_Mayhem)

comments.author: 0bscuris
comments.body:
I think, it’s obviously the future. The easier traditional games are to make the more they will get buried in clones. If ur doing game design and ur not thinking about how to use ai to innovate on design, i think ur limiting ur potential. 

There is a couple hurdles though: 

hardware demands are high, i stopped playing triple a games years ago and indie games don’t usually have high enough fidelity graphics to demand powerful gpu’s so i could use my old card without asking too much of it. ai games will need better hardware, if u add that ontop of high fidelity graphics hardware becomes a real issue. 

It’s still hard to set up and run, like irc chat vs facebook, the more difficult the technology is to set up, the more people ur going to lose. Setting up ollama, getting the games to work together, deciding which model to use and whatnot, all an issue. There is no standard yet. 

The point is, ai will become the standard. Once you have played a 4x strategy game where u negotiated a peace treaty with an ai, u’ll never wanna go back to clicking the auto balance gold button to make the number turn green and have the computer accept the deal.

replies.author: MakeEmMayhem
replies.body:
I do wonder if the first really successful AI-native games will be the ones that hide the technical complexity completely. Players probably should not need to think about models, setup, or prompts. They should just feel like the game lets them do something they could not do before.

(by the way, is that an actual game?? the peace treaty with ai :O)

replies.author: 0bscuris
replies.body:
I think ur totally right that the process will be mostly hidden. You don’t really realize how many different ways there is to write a jump function and how they feel as a player, u just know it’s good or bad. It’s only when u start messing around under the hood u learn that stuff. 

Not a game yet, just a concept. I have playtested using grok and grok skills to try to work the concept but i havn’t sat down and written the scripts needed to maintain it. The trickiness of llm is that it needs boundries that are loose enough that it feels natural but tight enough that it doesn’t run amok. 

The biggest weakness to llm is thst it is so fast at producing lots that people will just send it, really what makes it good is the testing and iterating part. Like, minimum i’d need 50-60 negotiations in playtesting to really feel how it works.

replies.author: MakeEmMayhem
replies.body:
This is super close to what we’re wrestling with too.

Small disclosure: I’m working on Make ’Em Mayhem, an AI-native roguelike autobattler where players generate characters and then build a team around who those characters become.

And yeah, the tricky part is not getting AI to produce wild ideas. That part is enjoyable. The tricky part is putting enough structure around it so the output becomes actual gameplay: roles, abilities, drawbacks, synergies, counters, etc.

I really like how you described it. Loose enough to feel natural, tight enough not to run amok is basically the whole design challenge.

replies.author: 0bscuris
replies.body:
Yeah, makes total sense. We already had procedural generation for stats but the characters were only ever skin deep.

If you take something like disgea style games, u got ur five or so named characters that have personalities and then an army of guys who are all just a name and a color and stat block.

Generating stat blocks, leveling, formulating battle plans, traditional code can handle that, it’s just math and probability.

What it can’t do is sit around the campfire and talk to you. Let’s take something like mass effect, in traditional code, you choose between kaiden and ashley, a bool gets flipped, that bool gets tracked and when it generates a scene later, it checks the bool and if it’s kaiden it puts in kaiden and his dialogue and if it’s ashley, the opposite.

But garrus can’t die, cuz they didn’t write any dialogue to replace him. They didn’t code in the other characters reactions. You get one very important choice, one time.

Llm blows the doors off that.

U can procedurally generate a new stat block to replace garrus and then use traditional code asking the llm and tweaking the outputs to follow ur rules, to generate a new team mate and that team mate’s dialogue is not limited to precoded strings with audio files.

Now ur play through and mine arn’t like 10% different because i saved ashley and u saved kaiden and there was a few dialogue trees that are affected. Now our play throughs are 70-80% different because a character that doesn’t even exist in ur instance, is my most important npc.

Edit: by the way, game video looks great.

replies.author: MakeEmMayhem
replies.body:
Aww!! Thank you so much for your compliment! :))

I hope you liked the game (the playtest is available for free). Would really appreciate your support if you could wishlist it and share it with friends that you think will enjoy this too!

comments.author: Nez_Coupe
comments.body:
Man I went wild with an idea maybe 6 months back for an actual AI rpg, isometric style. Basically there was a set amount of highest-class items that could be made, stored, etc. but there could be infinite subclasses made from those. You started in a small area with fog all around, which blocks you, and there are like “state thresholds” which allow for gen ai to have enough context through storytelling and current-area exploration to generate the new area parameters. I went hard for a month. Pretty much almost got psychosis. The idea I had was a good idea I think, but I’d need a team of people to implement what I had in mind. Everything was independent but also dependent, where say, and innkeeper my just randomly bring up something about an outcast that he saw pass by, and elf, and later that becomes a detail to push the world state into the large “area creation” transitions, and the game might use the context to generate the outcast somewhere on the new map through the archetype npc() class and create a subclass for it and render it somewhere to be interacted with.

I don’t know. It was crazy, but interesting. Wish I had a partner on it or a small team, it might have went somewhere.

replies.author: Life-Animator-3658
replies.body:
Interesting in theory. But I can’t imagine that’s feasible yet. The tech is there for sure. But to accomplish that you’d have to use frontier models and/or local models around 120B for reliable results. Frontier models no consumer would want to pay for to use their APIs, and no one has strong enough gaming PCs to run local models capable of reliable results. 

We’re still a tech leap away from that IMO. Once we can run models that take up 8GB VRAM and output reliable results then we’re talking. It’s a really cool idea though. I’d say keep developing it and hope the tech catches up. You’d be one of the firsts

replies.author: Nez_Coupe
replies.body:
It’s really not. It was fun mess around with. You’d need so much infrastructure to run a local model or pay for the api. It worked… a little bit. I was doing it as a POC. So yea, I agree with you. 

It’s parked for the foreseeable future.

replies.author: MakeEmMayhem
replies.body:
I think both of you are pointing at the real bottleneck!

The tech can generate impressive things, but making those things reliable, persistent, affordable, and gameable is much harder.

The outcast elf example is cool because it is not just random generation. It implies continuity: a small detail from one conversation becomes part of the next region and maybe later becomes a character the player can meet.

But that creates a whole design burden:

\- what details enter world state?

\- which ones are just flavor?

\- how much can the game remember?

\- what happens if the model contradicts itself?

\- how do you keep costs sane????????

That’s where I think AI-native games will need strong constraints, not just stronger models.

comments.author: TaylorCooper337
comments.body: I would define "AI Native" as having a model built into the game to handle certain aspects, whether npcs, world events, etc.   Once an AI model is bundled/connected into the main logic of the game (This could be API calls too), that game is natively/necessarily AI.
